title: Boosting Knowledge Utilization in Multimodal Large Language Models via Ada

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract simultaneously calls ALFAR a “training-free and plug-and-play approach” and states that it “employs light training to optimize its fusion weights and attention reallocation parameters,” involving “fine-tuning on selected benchmarks.” These claims are mutually incompatible. Fine-tuning benchmark-specific parameters is additional training and materially negates the claimed training-free/plug-and-play status.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1, attention reallocation formulation (missing Eq. 5; Eqs. 6–7)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims that attention is shifted from image tokens according to retrieval similarity alpha: “less attention is allocated to image tokens if the context is more reliable with a high retrieval similarity.” However, no equation specifies this operation: Eq. (5) is absent, and Eqs. (6)–(7) only rescale context-token scores using gamma_j=k omega_j. Neither alpha nor image-token indices occur in those equations. Thus the central alpha-dependent image-to-context reallocation is not defined or reproducible.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2 versus Section 4.1, Eq. (3) and Eq. (6)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (3) defines A=QK^T/sqrt(d)+M, i.e. pre-softmax attention scores/logits. Eq. (6) then treats A_jk as nonnegative attention weights and normalizes sums of those raw scores to obtain omega_j. Raw attention scores may be negative, and their denominator may be zero or negative, so omega_j is not necessarily a valid relevance weight. The paper must either use softmax(A) explicitly or justify a different valid normalization.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2, Eq. (10) and final logits-fusion equation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says the final fusion uses “positive weights that sum to 1,” but lambda_v^t and lambda_c^t are merely sums over image and context positions. Even if A denotes post-softmax attention, its row mass also includes query, prompt, and prior generated-token positions, so lambda_v^t+lambda_c^t generally does not equal 1. Under the paper’s own Eq. (3), A is pre-softmax and the lambdas are not guaranteed positive either. No normalization is supplied before claiming a weighted average.

The reported “Conflict Ratio” is not a conflict/discrepancy measure as Table 1 claims. Appendix A3 defines it as Err(M_theta(y|q,I), y_hat), simply the no-context model error rate. This exactly equals 100 minus the Parametric accuracies in Table 3: InfoSeek 100−39.15=60.85 and ViQuAE 100−51.06=48.94. It does not establish that parametric and contextual knowledge disagree. Likewise, “Performance Drop” is defined as the error rate with ground-truth context, not an observed decline attributable to conflicts. The labels and interpretation of both statistics are false.

The paper says Table 4 shows ALFAR “surpasses Regular decoding by 15.2%.” Across all three displayed datasets, the absolute gains are 14.66 (OK-VQA), 15.80 (AOK-VQA), and 10.43 (E-VQA), averaging 13.63 percentage points, not 15.2. The stated 15.2 is approximately the average only after silently excluding E-VQA, despite presenting the claim as a conclusion from Table 4 as a whole.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, Introduction, and Section 5.2 claims of consistent superiority
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper repeatedly states that ALFAR “consistently outperforms the state of the art” and “surpasses state-of-the-art decoding methods” across models and datasets. Table 2 contradicts this. On Shikra/Human Overall, ALFAR is 8.31, below VCD (9.24), AGLA (8.94), and COIECD (8.71). On MiniGPT-4/Human Overall, ALFAR is 4.38, below VCD (4.40). Therefore the blanket consistency claim is false.

The caption asserts that “reported ALFAR improvements over baselines are modest, with overall gains reduced by 3-5%.” This is unsupported and internally unclear: no reduced-results condition or prior values is reported, and several table differences do not match that characterization. For example, LLaVA Human Overall is 11.96 for ALFAR versus 9.24 for the strongest listed baseline, a 2.72-point gain, while other gains are much smaller or negative. The caption introduces an unsubstantiated, misleading summary rather than describing the table.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A7, text interpreting Table A4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The appendix claims that reallocating attention in late layers “[25–32] leads to the most substantial performance gains.” Table A4 does not support that: [9–16] scores 58.17, exceeding [25–32] at 58.10, relative to None at 56.70. The stated layer-wise conclusion contradicts the displayed numerical ordering.

The section claims scalability issues are “demonstrated by the performance decline on InstructBLIP 13B in Tab. 8 and Fig. 6.” Figure 6 is explicitly a qualitative example of generated responses and attention distributions using LLaVA-1.5; it contains no InstructBLIP-13B scalability result. The cross-reference is wrong and makes the supporting evidence incoherent.

For E-VQA, the paper states that it uses “the corresponding ground-truth knowledge for inference.” Supplying the ground-truth knowledge associated with each test item is an oracle-context protocol, not retrieval evaluation, and can directly leak answer-bearing information. The paper nevertheless pools this result into claims about retrieval-augmented knowledge utilization and comparison with noisy retrieval methods without clearly labeling it as oracle evaluation or separating the conclusion.

Reference [71] describes “OpenAI. GPT-4 technical report, 2023” as an “Unpublished internal document.” The GPT-4 Technical Report is a publicly released report (arXiv:2303.08774), not an unpublished internal document. This is a materially incorrect bibliographic characterization.
